text:
Okay, thanks. I found Q3 pretty tough – balancing privacy and usefulness felt…real. It's easy to say ‘never’ to things like age or ethnicity, but that feels overly cautious when the goal is *help*. I answered “small” for disability data because my own experiences with ADHD mean early intervention could have made a huge difference, but it absolutely needs safeguards.

I think Q5 – fairness versus accuracy – is crucial. Losing 5% accuracy to make things equitable? Absolutely worth it. The biggest divergence seemed to be around Absalon data (Q3.4). I opted for ‘moderate’ because tracking page views feels…intrusive, but maybe other students feel differently about that level of monitoring. Perhaps an opt-out would address that tension – let people choose what's shared?

Thanks. I agree with S4 about Q3 being difficult - it *is* real! I found the framing helpful though, knowing it was just for support and privacy would be protected. I also chose “moderate” for Absalon data; it feels like a step too far to monitor what pages students access. Though I see the logic of improving prediction, at what cost?

Q4 – explainability - felt most important. As someone navigating health issues impacting my studies, needing to *understand* why support is offered is vital. I think the strong consensus on losing accuracy for fairness (Q5) is good; it shows we’re prioritizing equity. My divergence was probably around disability data – while I answered “small” due to personal experience, others might understandably be more wary. Perhaps a tiered consent system?

Thanks both of you. I agree with S3 and S4 - Q3 *was* really tough, that balance feels…precarious. Coming from outside Denmark originally, and having restarted my degree, I’m acutely aware of how easily systems can unintentionally disadvantage certain groups. That's why I was stricter on nationality and financial aid – even a 'small' improvement needs strong justification given the potential for bias.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely key. Because I *did* drop out once, understanding why this model flags me, or suggests support, will be critical to whether I trust it. The opt-out idea for Absalon data is good, and maybe even a general ‘pause’ button on the whole system – if students are uncomfortable, they need control. My biggest divergence was probably with accepting *any* improvement for sensitive data; I leaned towards "never" more often than most, given my experiences feeling like an outsider navigating a new system.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really challenging too – that tension between helping more students and respecting privacy felt very real. As someone who *did* drop out before, I understand needing support, but also feel strongly about data security. I went with “small” improvements for things like first-generation status and financial aid because those factors can absolutely impact access to resources, but it needs careful handling.

I think Q4 – explainability – is vital. Honestly, if this model flags me *again*, knowing *why* is crucial. The consensus on fairness (Q5) is reassuring. I differed a bit on Absalon data; "small" felt okay as long as there’s transparency about what's tracked and why. An opt-out or ‘pause’ button, like S6 suggested, would definitely increase my trust.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said – Q3 was particularly difficult for me as an advisor. It’s easy to *want* more data to improve identification, but we have to be incredibly careful about crossing lines. From my perspective, that means erring on the side of caution, especially with sensitive demographics.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely crucial. We need to be able to justify why a student is flagged to both them *and* to colleagues if we’re going to build trust. I differed slightly – leaning towards ‘moderate’ improvements for Absalon data, provided it's transparent and opt-out is available. It might flag engagement issues impacting performance.

The tiered consent system suggested by S3 sounds excellent; a good compromise could be valuable here.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A2 – Q3 *was* deeply uncomfortable, balancing potential benefit against significant privacy concerns. As an advisor, I see students struggling, and want to reach them early, but it's incredibly important we don’t inadvertently reinforce inequalities through this model. My answers reflected that caution; moderate improvements needed strong justification, especially with Absalon data.

I think Q4 – explainability – is the most vital question here. Students need to understand *why* they’ve been flagged, and as advisors we need to be able to articulate that clearly. The opt-out suggestions are excellent. I diverged slightly on first-generation status (moderate), as I see its impact regularly, but even then, it needs careful consideration – a tiered consent system would absolutely be beneficial.

Thanks everyone. Q3 felt really difficult; honestly, pretty stressful. As someone with dyslexia who’s just started uni, I'm already hyper-aware of being *seen* as different. So adding more data points feels risky – even if it helps others, what about me? I went with ‘moderate’ for course performance and Absalon, but only if there's a clear benefit.

I think Q4 is massively important. Knowing *why* the model thinks I'm struggling…that matters hugely. It needs to be tied into my support plan. The opt-out idea is great; control feels essential. My biggest divergence was probably disability data – I said moderate, because acknowledging that impacts me directly, but understand others are wary of being labelled. A tiered consent system sounds perfect - let us choose what's shared!

Thanks everyone, it’s really good to hear so many thoughtful responses. I definitely agree with S4 and S6 about Q3 being incredibly difficult – that balance between help and privacy feels very fragile, especially as an international student still settling in. I leaned towards “small” improvements for nationality and first-gen status because those experiences *can* create challenges, but it needs to be handled carefully. 

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely vital, as S3 pointed out. Understanding *why* the model flags me is crucial; just knowing isn’t enough – I need to see how it connects to my situation and what support is available. The tiered consent system sounds like a really good solution to address some of these anxieties around data sharing and control.

Thanks everyone, it’s helpful to hear such varied perspectives. I agree with S3 and A2 – Q3 felt particularly fraught. As someone finishing my Masters a bit later than expected, *and* dealing with a long-term mental health condition, the idea of more data collection feels…vulnerable. I chose ‘small’ for nationality and disability because those factors genuinely impact access to support, but even then, strong safeguards are essential. 

I think Q4 – explainability – is paramount. Knowing *why* this model flags me isn't just about trust, it's about understanding how the university sees my situation and tailoring support effectively. The tiered consent system feels crucial; I need agency over what’s shared, especially given my health condition. I strongly support prioritizing fairness even if it means slightly lower overall accuracy – leaving people behind is unacceptable.

Thanks everyone. It’s been really interesting to hear all these perspectives. I definitely agree Q3 was the toughest – balancing help and privacy feels incredibly delicate. Coming from outside the EU and working while studying, financial aid *does* impact my ability to focus, so a ‘small’ improvement felt acceptable, but only with strong safeguards against bias.

I think explainability (Q4) is hugely important; understanding *why* I'm flagged will dictate whether I trust the system enough to engage with support. The opt-out and tiered consent ideas are excellent – control feels vital for building that trust. I also strongly agree prioritising fairness, even if it means identifying slightly fewer students overall. It’s about equitable access to help, not just maximizing numbers.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said – Q3 was really difficult, especially given my own experience dropping out once. It made me think about why *I* struggled, and how easily things can fall through the cracks. That’s why I leaned towards ‘small’ improvements for first-gen status and financial aid – those barriers are real. 

For me, Q4, explainability, is essential. Because I restarted my degree, being flagged again would be…intimidating. Knowing *why* it happened, understanding the reasoning, that would make a huge difference in whether I'd even consider reaching out for help. The tiered consent system sounds fantastic - letting students control what’s shared feels really important to build trust.

Thanks everyone, that was a very insightful round – I particularly appreciate hearing perspectives from students about vulnerability and control. As an advisor, Q3 *was* incredibly difficult; it’s easy to get caught up in wanting more data for better identification, but we must prioritize student wellbeing and privacy above all else. 

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely critical. We need a system where flagging a student isn't just about identifying risk, but facilitating *meaningful* conversations – explaining the ‘why’ is crucial for both building trust and providing effective support. The tiered consent system seems like an excellent compromise, offering agency to students while still allowing us to proactively reach out when needed. I agree with others that fairness needs to be a core principle.
